title: Borrowed sounds: ג׳ ז׳ צ׳
topic: the geresh: ג׳ (j as in “jam”), ז׳ (s as in “measure”), צ׳ (ch as in “chip”); loanwords
why: The geresh lets you write the sounds dj, j and tch, which Hebrew doesn't have, and opens the door to the many international words of everyday Israeli life. You also learn to write your own name in Hebrew, just before the big alef-bet review.

The geresh: a little mark that changes the sound

Hebrew has no letter for the j in \"jeans\", for the s in \"pleasure\" or for the ch in \"chips\". For words from other languages, you add a little mark after the letter, the geresh (׳). In our transliteration, dj is the j of \"jeans\", j is the s of \"pleasure\", and tch is the ch of \"chips\":

LetterNameSoundExample
ג׳gimel + gereshdj, like the j in \"jeans\"גִ׳ינְס djins, jeans
ז׳zayin + gereshj, like the s in \"pleasure\"זָ׳קֶט jaket, a jacket
צ׳tsadi + gereshtch, like the ch in \"chips\"צִ׳יפְּס tchips, French fries

The vowel stays under the letter, and the geresh goes right after it: גִ׳ is read dji. Without the geresh, you get the usual sounds back: ג = g, ז = z, צ = ts.

On a phone, Israelis often type a simple apostrophe: ג'ינס. It's the same word.

", "

International words

Lots of everyday words are international: you read them, and you understand them right away.

HebrewSoundMeaning
פִּיצָהpitsapizza
טַקְסִיtaksitaxi
אוֹטוֹבּוּסotobusbus
בַּנְקbankbank
אִינְטֶרְנֶטinternetinternet
סְטוּדֶנְט / סְטוּדֶנְטִיתstudent / studentitstudent (m. / f.)
אוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָהuniversitauniversity

Where an English speaker slips up: many of these words came into Hebrew through Russian, German or other European languages, not through English. So you say מוּזִיקָה (muzika), with a z sound and a final a, and שׁוֹקוֹלָד (shokolad), with sh and a clearly pronounced final d. And a borrowed word takes the Hebrew feminine: סְטוּדֶנְטִית.

אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְטִית בָּאוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה.I'm a student at the university. (a woman is speaking) [ani studentit ba-universita.]

Your name in Hebrew

A foreign name is written the way it's pronounced, with the closest Hebrew letters. Here are some French names (like Léo's):

NameIn HebrewSound
Julieז׳וּלִיJuli: j = ז׳
Georgesז׳וֹרְז׳Jorj: ז׳ twice
CharlesשַׁרְלSharl: the French ch = שׁ
MichelמִישֶׁלMishel
LéoלֵאוֹLéo

Write what you hear, not how the name is spelled in English: in French, the ch of \"Charles\" sounds like sh, so it needs no geresh, שׁ already makes that sound. The English Charles, with the ch of \"chips\", would take tsadi + geresh; John and Jessica start with gimel + geresh (dj). The geresh is only for dj, j and tch. And the French u (in Julie) doesn't exist in Hebrew: Julie becomes \"Zhoo-lee\" [Juli].

אֲנִי ז׳וּלִי, מִפָּרִיז.I'm Julie, from Paris. [ani Juli, mi-Pariz.]

The same little mark is also used to write numbers with letters: יוֹם א׳ (yom alef) is Sunday, the first day of the Israeli week.
